Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim

Surat al-Buruj

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾

Al-buruj (constellations, mansions of the stars) is the plural of burj (tower, constellation). Scholars differed over what is meant here: are they the manazil (stations of the moon), or the kawakib (stars), or palaces in the sky guarded by watchers?

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already explained this in Surat al-Hijr, in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Hijr: 16], and in Surat al-Furqan, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed therein a lamp and a moon giving light﴾ [al-Furqan: 61].

It has been said that the root of this word is from manifestness (zuhur), and from it comes tabarruj (a woman displaying her adornment). He also presented an explanation of the intended meaning of the constellations of the sky and the number of the mansions mentioned.

As for the connection between the surahs, some exegetes say: when He mentioned the fate of the two groups and the scattering of the scrolls in the previous surah, He here mentioned one of the most severe deeds of the disbelievers against the believers, in the story of the trench (al-ukhdud).

What appears stronger than this, and Allah knows best, is that when He had previously mentioned the splitting of the sky, the scattering of the stars, the rending of the sky, and its hearkening to its Lord and its right to do so, He here came to explain the true nature of this sky: that it is great in structure with its vast towers, or its great constellations. Despite that, it obeys its Lord and submits, and it splits and bursts asunder because of the terror of that Day. So you, O human being, are more deserving (of obedience). And Allah knows best.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the promised day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun), and they were promised it in the worldly life. Thus it is the day promised to each of the two groups, as Allah, exalted is He, said concerning the believers: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them, [saying], "This is your day which you were promised."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103], and concerning the disbelievers: (p-477) ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play until they meet their day which they are promised.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 83]. They will acknowledge this at the resurrection (al-ba'th), when they say: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52].

So the promised day is the Day of Resurrection, the day promised for the recompense of both groups for their deeds.

Surah al-Buruj

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the promised day﴾.

The reconciliation between this and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ has already been discussed (taqaddama wajhu al-jam'i baynahu wa-bayna qawlihi).

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 3:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the witness and the witnessed﴾

Here he does not state explicitly who the witness (shahid) is or what the witnessed (mashhud) is. The word "shahid" is used in the Qur'an in the sense of "one who is present," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [al-An'am: 73].

"Mashhud" is used in the sense of "mushahad" (that which is seen) in the form of the passive participle, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day that will be witnessed﴾ [Hud: 103].

So the witness and the witnessed may both derive from "mushahadah" (seeing/being present). The witness may also derive from "shahadah" (testimony), and the witnessed may be one to whom or against whom testimony is given, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41].

Thus "shahid" in the first instance means a witness over the nation to which he was sent, and "shahid" in the second instance means a witness over the messengers concerning their nations.

From this point, the views of the exegetes have differed to about twenty opinions.

Ibn Jarir said, in summary: The witness is the day of Friday, and the witnessed is the day of 'Arafah or the day of sacrifice (al-Nahr). He attributed this to 'Ali and Abu Hurayrah. The witness is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. He attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali. The witness is the human being, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection; he attributed this to Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. The witness is Allah, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection; he attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas. Then he said: "The correct view in my opinion is that it is applicable to everything that may be called 'mushahid' (present) and may be called 'mashhud' (witnessed), and he did not distinguish whether it is in the sense of presence or of testimony." Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir were of the same view.

(p-478) Abu Hayyan, however, made a distinction as we have mentioned, and said: If it is in the sense of presence, then the witness is the human being and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. When He mentioned the promised Day, it was appropriate to mention everyone who bears witness on that Day and everyone against whom witness is borne. He mentioned about twenty views.

He said: "Each has its basis. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that it is from the category of testimony, because mention of the promised Day suffices in place of the witnessed Day. Rather, that Day needs someone to bear witness in it, and testimony is established concerning what will be presented on it, in order to establish proof against the creatures, not to establish the truth."

The Qur'an has mentioned the enumeration of witnesses on that Day, in a manner that fits with the presentation (al-'ard) and the reckoning (al-hisab).

In sum, the testimony is specific, general, and more general than general. From the specific is the testimony of the body parts against a person, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their eyes, and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat: 20], and His saying: ﴿This Day We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness concerning what they used to earn﴾ [Ya-Sin: 65]. This is testimony of action and speech, not testimony of state (hal), as His saying concerning them clarifies: ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why do you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned." ﴿And you did not conceal [yourselves] so that your hearing and your eyes and your skins would not testify against you, but you assumed that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾ [Fussilat: 21-22]. Allah refuted their claim with His saying: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you, and you have become among the losers﴾ [Fussilat: 23].

The shaykh (al-Shinqiti) has previously explained the testimony of the limbs in Surah Ya-Sin and in Surah al-Nisa' at His saying: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah a [single] statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. Also the testimony of the angels, who are the recording angels (al-hafazah), as in His saying: ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is with me, ready [to be recorded]"﴾ [Qaf: 23], and His saying: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. Then the testimony of the messengers, each messenger over his nation, as in His saying concerning 'Isa, upon him and upon our Prophet be the best of prayers and peace: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. This, although it is during his life, he will fulfill it on the Day of Resurrection.

And as in His saying concerning the nations in general: ﴿And [mention] the Day We will raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 89].

(p-479) From it: the testimony of the Messenger (ﷺ) over all the messengers, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41].

From it: the testimony of this nation over the rest of the nations, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a just nation that you may be witnesses over the mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

From it: the testimony of the Messenger (ﷺ) over this nation, according to His saying: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

From it: the testimony of Allah, exalted is He, over all.

This is what fits with the mention of the promised Day and what will occur in it of recompense and reckoning for deeds, and the requiting of creatures for them. And in the same context will come His saying: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness﴾ [al-Buruj: 9]. And it, as you see, is not restricted to one witness, and also one part of them does not contradict another.

So the difference of witnesses and their multiplicity is according to the difference and multiplicity of the one against whom testimony is given, from an individual, to a nation, to messengers, and to other than that. All of them are included in the meaning and actually occur.

Other views have been mentioned, but they are not specific to the Day of Resurrection.

From them: that the witness is Allah, the angels, and those of knowledge, and the witnessed-to is the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

From them: the witness is the created things, and the witnessed-to is the power of Allah, exalted is He, so that testimony here means a sign (al-'alamah).

The most prolific of the exegetes in this regard is al-Fakhr al-Razi, since he presented all of them with their proofs, except for what we have mentioned from the Sunnah, which he did not include.

The Sunnah has specified testimonies other than what has been mentioned.

From them is the testimony for the muezzin: "No tree, nor stone, nor clay hears his voice, except that it will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection."

(p-480) From them is the testimony of the earth against a person concerning what he did upon it, which is alluded to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day it will report its news﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 4].

From them: the testimony of wealth against its owner concerning how he spent it. From them: the testimony of fasting and the Qur'an and their intercession for their companions, and similar. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

**Note**

In this presentation there is an indication related to the judgment and the perfection of justice. Since the Lord of Majesty, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is over all things a Witness, and with all things Knowing, and has appointed guardians who record the deeds of the servants, yet He does not judge among the creatures by what He knows of them, nor by what His angels have recorded; and He causes their limbs to speak, and calls the messengers to witness against the nations, and the Messenger (ﷺ) to witness against the messengers, meaning that they conveyed the messages of Allah to their nations, then the judge should not judge by his own knowledge all the more so. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

It has been reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "You bring your disputes to me, and I am only a human being. I judge for you according to what I hear. So whoever I give him something from the right of his brother, then I am only giving him a piece of Fire." The hadith... That is: it was possible that revelation would descend to him, especially in that very case, since they spoke of inheritances whose markers had been effaced and there was no clear evidence (bayyinah) between them. But if revelation descended to him (ﷺ) concerning them, then who, by revelation, will [decide] for those who come after him in judgment?

For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "The clear evidence (bayyinah) is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the one who denies."

It is well known that "bayyinah" is a form derived from "bayan" (clarification), so it includes everything that clarifies the truth, whether testimony or circumstantial evidence (qara'in), as in the story of Yusuf, with the circumstantial evidences regarding his brothers and regarding the wife of al-'Aziz. Etc.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench, the fire full of fuel﴾.

Abu Hayyan said: The response to the oath in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿By the sky containing the mansions of the stars﴾ has been said to be omitted. It was said: it is "You will surely be resurrected" and the like. It was said: it is mentioned, and it was said: it is ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10] and the like. It was said: it is "Destroyed (qutila)," and this is what we prefer. The lam was omitted, meaning "Surely destroyed (laqutila)," and its omission is good, just as it is good in His saying: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [ash-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ [ash-Shams: 9], meaning "Indeed he has succeeded." The response serves as evidence of the curse of Allah upon the one who did that, and as a warning to the disbelievers of Quraysh who harm the believers in order to turn them away from their religion.

If "qutila" is the response, then it is a declarative sentence; if the response is other than it, then it is an imperative sentence, an invocation against them.

It was recited as "quttila" with the doubled letter; al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam recited it so, and the majority recited it with the single letter. End of quote.

Al-Ukhdud is the plural of khadd, which is a long cleft in the earth. His saying: ﴿the fire full of fuel﴾: al-Waquud is with a damma and with a fatha, and the recitation with a fatha is like as-sahur and al-wadu'. With a fatha: what one kindles with it, like sabur, and the water with which one performs ablution, and the food with which one eats the pre-dawn meal. With a damma: the verbal noun and the verb; al-wuqud with a damma is what one kindles with.

The author of al-Qamus mentioned that ﴿the fire full of fuel﴾ is a substitute (badal) for al-Ukhdud.

Several sayings have been reported regarding its meaning, to the point that Abu Hayyan said: "I grew weary of transmitting them."

Al-Fakhr al-Razi transmitted three of them.

The well-known account according to Ibn Kathir is what Ahmad and Muslim narrated, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Among those who came before you there was a king, and he had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he said to the king: 'I have grown old, and my time has come, so send me a boy to teach him sorcery.' So he sent him a boy whom he taught sorcery. Between the sorcerer and the king there was a monk. The boy came to the monk and heard his speech, and it pleased him. Whenever he went to the sorcerer, he would beat him and say: 'What has detained you?' And when he went to his family, they would beat him and say: 'What has detained you?' He complained of that to the monk, who said: 'When the sorcerer intends to beat you, say: "My family detained me," and when your family intends to beat you, say: "The sorcerer detained me."' Then one day, while he was there, he came upon a huge, fearsome beast that had blocked the people, so they could not pass. He said: 'Today I will know whether the matter of the monk is more beloved to Allah or the matter of the sorcerer.' He took a stone and said: 'O Allah, if the matter of the monk is more beloved to You and more pleasing to You than the matter of the sorcerer, then kill this beast so that the people may pass.' He threw it and killed it, and the people passed. He informed the monk of that, and the monk said: 'O my son, you are better than I am, and you will be tested. If you are tested, do not point to me.' The boy used to heal the blind and the leper and all other ailments and cure them. A blind companion of the king heard of him and brought him many gifts, saying: 'Cure me.' He said: 'I do not cure anyone; it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who cures. If you believe in Him, I will call upon Allah and He will cure you.' So he believed, and he called upon Allah and He cured him. Then he came to the king and sat in his usual place. The king said to him: 'O so-and-so, who restored your sight?' He said: 'My Lord.' He said: 'I?' He said: 'No, my Lord and your Lord is Allah.' He said: 'Do you have a lord other than me?' He said: 'Yes, my Lord and your Lord is Allah.' He continued to torture him until he pointed to the boy. The boy was brought, and the king said: 'O my son, your sorcery has reached the point that you heal the blind and the leper and these ailments.' He said: 'As for me, I do not cure anyone; it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who cures.' He said: 'I?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Do you have a lord other than me?' He said: 'My Lord and your Lord is Allah.' So he tortured him also until he pointed to the monk. The monk was brought, and it was said to him: 'Turn back from your religion,' but he refused. So they placed the saw at the middle of his head until it split into two halves. Then it was said to the blind man: 'Turn back from your religion,' but he refused, so they placed the saw at his middle as well. Then it was said to the boy: 'Turn back from your religion,' but he refused. So he sent him with a group of men to a mountain of such and such, and said: 'When you reach its summit, if he turns back from his religion, well and good; otherwise, throw him down.' They took him, and when they had climbed the mountain with him, he said: 'O Allah, suffice me against them by whatever You will.' The mountain shook beneath them, and they all fell down. The boy came walking until he entered upon the king, who said: 'What has your companions done?' He said: 'Allah, the Exalted, has sufficed me against them.' So he sent him with a group to the sea in a small boat, and said: 'When you have taken him out into the sea, if he turns back from his religion, well and good; otherwise, drown him.' The boy said: 'O Allah, suffice me against them by whatever You will.' So they drowned. The boy came and entered upon the king and said to him: 'You will not kill me until you do what I command you.' He said: 'What is it?' He said: 'Gather the people into one open plain, then crucify me on a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver, and say: "In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy." If you do that, you will kill me.' He did so, and he placed the arrow in his bow and shot him in the temple. The boy put his hand upon the place of the arrow and died. The people said: 'We believe in the Lord of the boy.' It was said to the king: 'Have you seen what you were fearing? By Allah, it has befallen you; all the people have believed.' So he commanded that trenches be dug at the mouths of the lanes, and fires were kindled in them, and he said: 'Whoever turns back from his religion, leave him; otherwise, throw him into them.' They continued to press and push one another. Then a woman came with a child she was nursing, and it seemed she hesitated to fall into the fire. The infant said: 'Be patient, O mother, for you are upon the truth.'" It has been said that the boy was buried and was found in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab with his hand upon his temple; whenever it was lifted, blood came out of his wound, and when it was left, it returned to the wound.

We have cited this account, and it is among the finest of what has come in this meaning, because of the lessons in it, and because some rulings may be derived from it. Since Ibn Kathir attributed it to Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Muslim, meaning that its chain is sound, it is traced back to the Prophet ﷺ. From it come the following:

First: that sorcery is learned by study, as in the account of the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut, who taught people sorcery.

Second: the possibility of good and evil coexisting when a person is ignorant of the reality of the evil, such as the coexistence of faith with the monk and the learning of sorcery from the sorcerer.

Third: the occurrence of extraordinary events at the hands of callers to good, to show the truth and to strengthen resolve in the matter, as the boy said: "Today I will know whether the matter of the monk is more beloved to Allah or the matter of the sorcerer?"

Fourth: that his heart leaned more toward the matter of the monk, since he said: "O Allah, if the matter of the monk is more beloved to You," so he asked about the matter of the monk and did not ask about the matter of the sorcerer.

Fifth: the acknowledgment by a scholar of the virtue of one who is superior to him, as the monk acknowledged the boy's superiority.

Sixth: the testing of those who call to Allah and the obligation of patience in that, and the variation in people's ranks in that.

Seventh: the attribution of the whole act to Allah: "It is Allah who cures."

Eighth: the caller to Allah's refusal of a wage for his work and his guidance: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it, if not﴾ [al-An'am: 90].

Ninth: the explanation of a fundamental pillar in the question of tawassul, which is that its basis is faith in Allah, then supplication and asking Allah, may He be exalted.

Tenth: the foolishness of the polytheist king, whose heart was closed by the darkness of shirk, for he supposed in himself that he was the one who cured his companion, though he had done nothing for him, and how could he be, when he does not know?

Eleventh: resorting to violence and brutality when unable to persuade and make understood is the method of the ignorant and the tyrants.

Twelfth: the utmost cruelty and harshness in killing a human being, without leniency.

Thirteenth: the utmost patience and not turning back from the religion; thus it was among the earlier nations, and it shows Allah's favor upon this community, since it is permitted for it to utter what contradicts its belief while its heart remains content with faith.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The verse indicates that one compelled to disbelief under threat of great destruction should rather be patient with what he is threatened with, and that uttering the word of disbelief is like a concession in that. He said: al-Hasan narrated that Musaylimah took two men from among the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and said to one of them: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes," and he let him go. He said the same to the other, and he said: "No, rather you are a liar," so he killed him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "As for the one who was let go, he took the concession, and there is no blame upon him; as for the one who was killed, he took the better course, so congratulations to him."

The discussion of this question has preceded with our Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him.

Fourteenth: the answering of the boy's supplication and Allah's support for His believing servants: "O Allah, suffice me against them by whatever You will."

Fifteenth: sacrificing oneself in the way of spreading the call, since the boy guided the king to the method by which the boy could persuade people to believe in Allah, even though reaching that would cost his own life.

Sixteenth: the preservation of his body until the time of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, as an honor to the friends of Allah and to the callers, lest the earth consume their bodies.

Seventeenth: the establishment of the indication of God's power over resurrection.

Eighteenth: the life of the martyrs, evidenced by the presence of blood and the return of the hand to its place by a deliberate movement.

Nineteenth: the knowledge of that story among the people of Makkah, for they were told of it as a warning of the consequences of their deeds against the weak believers, as is clarified in the full account.

Twentieth: the speech of the suckling child in affirmation of the truth.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 6:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they were sitting over it﴾. Regarding the pronoun in His saying "they" (hum), and the pronoun in His saying "sitting" (quʿūd), there is a difference of opinion.

(p-485) It has been said: both refer back to those who were burned and seated over it (the trench).

And it has been said: both refer back to the disbelievers.

On this view, there is a difficulty in His saying "sitting over it," namely: how is it possible for them to sit upon the fire?

It has been said: the fire turned back upon them and burned them, so their sitting over it is literal.

And it has been said: it means sitting at its edge, just as you say "sitting upon the river" or "upon the well," meaning at its edge and around it, as one says "so-and-so alighted at the water of such-and-such," meaning at it.

Abu Hayyan cited the verse of al-A'sha:

"It is kindled for two shivering men who warm themselves at it, and the generous and the one who shaves his head [the guest] spend the night by the fire."

The proponent of the first view has relied on the saying of God, may He be exalted, later in the surah: ﴿So for them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], and said: "the Burning" is in this world, and "Hell" is in the Hereafter.

But in the verse there is an indication that the pronouns refer to the disbelievers who killed the believers and burned them, and that indication is His saying: ﴿Then they did not repent, so for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], where He arranged the mentioned punishment upon their not repenting, and used "thumma" (then), which denotes delay. This indicates that their own fire did not burn them as immediate retribution; rather they were given respite to repent of their hideous deed, and otherwise for them is the mentioned punishment in the Hereafter. And God knows best.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they, over what they were doing to the believers, were witnesses﴾

It means present, and it agrees with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they sat over it [in attendance]﴾ [al-Buruj: 6]. That is, they were present, watching the burning of the believers. This is an added rebuke for them, since they saw this sight with their own eyes, yet did not feel pity for them, nor take warning from their steadfastness."

﴿وَمَا نَقَمُوا مِنْهُمْ إِلَّا أَنْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ﴾

This is what is called *uslub al-madh bima yushbih al-dham* (the stylistic device of praising something in the form of blame). Its parallel in Arabic is the verse of the poet:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

(p. 486) Abu Hayyan also cited the verse of the poet Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"They did not resent in the Banu Umayyah anything except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

And the verse of another:

"There is no flaw in her except the squint of her eye, just as the eyes of the birds of 'inaq are squinting."

It is said *'ayn shakla'* (a squinting eye) when there is a small, slight redness in its whiteness.

We have already mentioned that their resentment against them is directed to the future, as in His saying: ﴿except that they believe in Allah﴾, not to the past, as in "except that they had believed," because they used to say to them: "Either you return from your religion, or you will be thrown into the Fire." They did not burn them for their past faith, but for their persistence in faith going forward.

The mention here of the two attributes of Allah, *al-'Aziz al-Hamid* ("the Almighty, the Praiseworthy"), indicates that He, glory be to Him, is able to support the believers and to take vengeance upon the disbelievers, since *al-'Aziz* is the Dominant, as they say: "Whoever is mighty plunders." However, the description of Him as *al-Hamid* came to convey two matters:

The first: that the believers believed out of both desire and fear: desire for the Praiseworthy, in accordance with what follows: ﴿al-Ghafur al-Wadud﴾ [al-Buruj: 14], and fear of the Almighty, as will come in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12]. This is the perfection of faith, with desire and fear, and the best state of the believer.

The second matter: so that those disbelievers would not despair of His bounty and mercy, as He said: ﴿then they did not repent﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], since He granted them respite as one of the effects of His attribute of Praiseworthiness, glory be to Him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾

This is an emphasis and an elucidation of "the Mighty, the Praiseworthy," since none goes outside His authority. He is the Subduer above His servants, and He is the one who manages the affair of His dominion, glorified and exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness﴾ is a connection to the beginning of the surah: ﴿And by the witness and the witnessed﴾ [al-Buruj: 3]. So He, glorified is He, is Witness over all things, and among that is the deed of those people. In this there is great intimidation of those people, a warning to them and to those who follow their course, that Allah, exalted is He, is Witness over their deeds, and nothing hidden will be concealed from Him.

It has come in the intensive form "Shahid" (Witness) because it suits this context, and in it there is also a correspondence with the verb, as they were sitting over the fire and were witnesses to the burning of the friends of Allah, exalted is He. So He, glorified is He, will requite them in kind, for He will burn them while He is Witness over them.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent﴾

It is possible that what is meant by this is the people of the trench (ashab al-ukhdud), and "fatanu" (persecuted) here means "burned." It is also possible that it is general, covering everyone who harmed the believers in order to seduce them away from their religion and turn them back from it, by whatever kinds of trial and torment.

Abu Hayyan preferred the latter view, and taking it in its general sense is more appropriate, so that it includes the disbelievers of Quraysh with the warning and threat, and directing them to repent of what they inflicted upon the weak among the believers, such as 'Ammar, Bilal, Suhayb, and others.

This generality is supported by the other generality that corresponds to it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great triumph﴾ [al-Buruj: 11]. This is general without any dispute, covering everyone who is characterized by these attributes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾, is in the position of what is stated being derived from what is implied in "the Mighty, the Praiseworthy", as has been previously mentioned.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾

It has been said: He originates creation and repeats it, as with crops, plants and humans, through birth and death, then through resurrection.

It has also been said: He begins the disbelievers' punishment and repeats it upon them. In support of this, they cite His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa: 56]

And in a hadith: "No owner of camels who does not pay their zakat will be spared, except that on the Day of Resurrection they will be laid down for him on a level plain, and they will come to him at their fattest, and they will trample him with their hooves and butt him with their horns. Whenever the last of them passes over him, the first of them will be brought back against him, until judgment is passed among the creatures and he sees his destination, either to Paradise or to the Fire." (p-488) to the end of the hadith concerning the owner of cattle, sheep and gold.

But what appears to be the case, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is the first view, because it recurs in the Qur'an, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it.﴾ [Yunus: 4] And His saying: ﴿Say, "Allah originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you deluded?"﴾ [Yunus: 34]

He made this a sign of His power, and a proof of the incapacity and deficiency of the partners, in His saying at the beginning of this verse: ﴿Say, "Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?"﴾ And He answered them with His saying: ﴿Say, "Allah originates creation and then repeats it,"﴾ and His saying: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We are ever doing it.﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 104]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the hosts, of Pharaoh and Thamud?﴾

After presenting the story of the People of the Trench, [the verse comes] as consolation and strengthening for the believers, and as a deterrent and rebuke for the polytheists. It brings reports about some of the nations that came before, Pharaoh and Thamud, as a substitution (badal) for "the hosts." "Hosts" is the plural of jund (soldiers, army), meaning multitudes and people of power. Its "story" (hadith) is what Allah related of its account concerning Musa and the Children of Israel.

As for the choice of Pharaoh here after the People of the Trench, it is due to the affinity and resemblance between them: Pharaoh transgressed and claimed lordship, like the king of the People of the Trench who said to his companion: "Is there a lord other than me?" It is also due to his torment of the Children of Israel by slaying the sons and sparing the women, and in that there was a great trial from your Lord. It is also due to the presentation of signs and proofs as evidence of the truth of the caller, for Musa, peace be upon him, presented to Pharaoh the great signs of his Lord, yet he denied and disobeyed. The boy presented to this king the great signs: the healing of the blind and the leper by Allah's permission. Pharaoh was unable to overcome Musa and reach him, and the king was unable to kill the boy, since Allah saved him from drowning and from being hurled from the top of the mountain. It was therefore fitting that he should have desisted from that and grasped the truth, but his dominion blinded him, just as it blinded Pharaoh.

Likewise the magicians believed when they saw the sign of Musa, and they fell down prostrate to Allah.

And so here the people believed in the Lord of the boy, and the king fell into what Pharaoh fell into, for Pharaoh gathered the magicians so that the people might witness the incapacity and power of Musa, but the situation turned against him. The first of the people to believe were the helpers of Pharaoh against Musa. Similarly here, the swiftest of the people to believe were those whom the king gathered to witness the killing of the boy.

Thus the appropriateness of mentioning Pharaoh rather than other transgressing nations before is evident, although there is admonition and lesson in all of them. But this is the pinnacle of inimitability in the Qur'anic narratives and its style. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Likewise Thamud, because of their manifestations of power and transgression. Allah also combined them together in Surat al-Fajr in His saying: ﴿And Thamud who hewed the rocks in the valley﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh, the lord of stakes﴾ [al-Fajr: 9-10]. Thus He combined them here: ﴿Pharaoh and Thamud﴾.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the hosts, of Pharaoh and Thamud?﴾

It is not hidden that there comes to mind an apparent contradiction between the word "hosts" (al-junud) and the word "Pharaoh," because Pharaoh was not a host but a single specific man.

The answer is evident: what is meant by Pharaoh is he and his people, and he was mentioned alone because they were followers of him and under his obedience.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 85, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial﴾

That is: persistent among all the nations. And it has preceded, in Surat al-Inshiqaq before it: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve deny﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 22].

Al-Kirmani said: Mahmud ibn Hamza ibn Nasr, Taj al-Qurra' (the crown of the reciters), in his book Asrar al-Takrar fi al-Qur'an (The Secrets of Repetition in the Qur'an): the variation is for the sake of observing the ends of verses and the fasilah (rhyme-endings). But the apparent meaning from the context in both places is observing the context, not the rhyme-endings of the verses, because in Surat al-Inshiqaq the address is to the polytheists: ﴿You will surely ride from state to state﴾ ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾ ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve deny﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19–22].

And in Surat al-Buruj, here, he mentioned the nations: Pharaoh, Thamud, the People of the Trench, and the polytheists of Makkah, then said: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial﴾ [al-Buruj: 19]. So this fits here, and that fits there. And Allah knows best.
